title: Mole and its Relation with Mass, Volume and Number of Particles
topicTitle: Mole and its relation with mass, volume and number of particles
notes: A mole is the SI unit of amount of substance. It is the amount of substance that contains exactly the same number of elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, formula units) as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12, that is **6.022 × 10²³** entities — the Avogadro number N_A. The mole is simply a counting unit, like 'dozen' or 'score', but on a scale suited to atoms and molecules: it links the invisible particle world with weighable masses.

$n=\frac{m}{M}$, where m is the mass in grams and M the molar mass (g mol⁻¹). Molar mass = relative atomic/molecular mass expressed in g mol⁻¹: 1 atom of carbon has a mass of 12 u (1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 1/12 the mass of one ¹²C atom), while 1 mole of carbon atoms has a mass of 12 g. Gram-atomic mass and gram-molecular mass are the mass of one mole of atoms and of molecules respectively. Example: 44 g of CO₂ = 1 mol = 6.022 × 10²³ molecules.

$n=\frac{N}{N_{A}}$; N = n × N_A. The number of *atoms* must be counted with care: 1 mol of H₂SO₄ contains 2 mol H atoms, 1 mol S, 4 mol O (7 mol of atoms in total, 6.022 × 10²³ H₂SO₄ molecules), while 1 mol of H₂ contains 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ atoms. Ions, electrons and formula units can also be counted in moles (1 mol of NaCl gives 1 mol Na⁺ + 1 mol Cl⁻).

For gases the mole relates to volume through Avogadro's law: 1 mol of any gas at STP (273.15 K, 1 atm) occupies 22.4 L, so $n=\frac{V\ (\text{at STP})}{22.4}$; at RTP (25 °C, 1 bar) the molar volume is ≈24.0 L. For any other conditions the ideal gas equation is used: $n=\frac{PV}{RT}$. Concentration extends the idea to solutions: $n=M_{\text{conc}}\times V_{\text{L}}$ (molarity × volume in litres).
• Core of every stoichiometric calculation: converting masses, gas volumes and numbers of particles into moles and back, so that the mole ratio of a balanced equation can be applied.
• Determination of relative atomic and molecular masses, molar volumes, vapour densities and Avogadro's constant; standardisation of solutions and titrations.

• Industry and pharmacy: calculating exact reactant quantities and costs for ammonia, sulphuric acid, cement or drug manufacture; agriculture: fertiliser dosage; environment: calculating CO₂ (44 g mol⁻¹) and pollutant emissions per tonne of fuel; medicine: expressing doses and concentrations in moles.
• The mole counts *specified entities*: '1 mol of oxygen' is ambiguous (O atoms or O₂ molecules?), so the entity must always be named; the mole is meaningless without it.
• Since the 2019 SI revision N_A is a defined number (6.02214076 × 10²³) rather than being tied to 12 g of ¹²C, so the earlier 'gram-atom' style definitions are outdated.

• Molar masses are based on **standard atomic weights**, which are average values for the natural isotopic composition and therefore carry an uncertainty (and vary slightly for elements such as boron, lithium and lead whose isotopic abundances differ with source). Exact work needs isotope-specific molar masses.

• The relation n = V/22.4 L holds only for gases at STP that behave ideally; for real gases and for other conditions PV = nRT must be used, and for associating gases the particle count differs from the formula count.

• The mole expresses *amount*, not concentration — molarity, molality and mole fraction are different measures; molarity in particular is temperature-dependent because volume changes with temperature.
• Mole-based stoichiometry cannot predict how fast a reaction goes, in which direction it proceeds, or what yield it gives; those come from kinetics, thermodynamics and equilibrium.
confusion: ❌ One mole of oxygen means 6.022 × 10²³ oxygen atoms always. ✅ It depends on the entity: 1 mol O atoms = 16 g, but 1 mol O₂ molecules = 32 g and contains 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ atoms.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is a relative number in u; molar mass is the mass of one mole in g mol⁻¹ (numerically equal for most purposes).
❌ One mole of a gas always occupies 22.4 L. ✅ Only at STP and only for an ideal gas.
❌ The mole is a mass unit. ✅ It is the SI unit of *amount of substance*; it is converted to mass through the molar mass.
❌ Avogadro's number can be measured to any precision. ✅ It is now a defined constant exactly equal to 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

universalFacts: 1 mole of water = 18 g = 18 mL of liquid, yet contains 6.022 × 10²³ molecules.
1 mole of any gas at STP = 22.4 L; at RTP ≈ 24 L.
Gram-atomic mass of any element contains 6.022 × 10²³ atoms; gram-molecular mass contains the same number of molecules.
examples: **Problem:** Number of moles and molecules in 4.9 g of H₂SO₄ (M = 98 g mol⁻¹). **Solution:** n = 4.9/98 = 0.05 mol; molecules = 0.05 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.011 × 10²²; total atoms = 7 × 3.011 × 10²² ≈ 2.1 × 10²³.
**Problem:** Volume at STP and number of molecules in 8 g of oxygen. **Solution:** n = 8/32 = 0.25 mol; V = 0.25 × 22.4 = 5.6 L; molecules = 0.25 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.506 × 10²³.
importantNotes: Always name the entity ('atoms', 'molecules', 'ions') when using the mole — a standard precision point.
Use the four-way conversion web m ↔ n ↔ N ↔ V (STP) as the working framework of every numerical.
For gases away from STP switch to PV = nRT rather than misusing 22.4 L.
summary: The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance, defined as the amount containing 6.022 × 10²³ elementary entities — the same number of atoms as are in 12 g of carbon-12. It links the invisible particle world to weighable masses through the relations n = m/M, n = N/N_A, n = V/22.4 L for a gas at STP (or n = PV/RT at other conditions) and n = molarity × volume in litres, and the mole ratio taken from a balanced equation then drives every stoichiometric calculation. Since the 2019 SI revision N_A is the exact defined value 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹, and the mole counts only specified entities, so '1 mol of oxygen' is meaningless unless atoms or O₂ molecules are named.
importantConcepts: Mole as the SI unit of amount of substance — a counting unit like a dozen or a score
Avogadro constant N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹, exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ since the 2019 SI revision
Relation with mass: n = m/M, with molar mass expressed in g mol⁻¹
Relation with particles: n = N/N_A, counting atoms, ions and formula units carefully
Relation with gas volume: 22.4 L per mole at STP and about 24.0 L at RTP
Relation with solutions: n = molarity × volume of solution in litres
importantStatements: One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ elementary entities, the number of atoms in 12 g of ¹²C.
One mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 L at STP (273.15 K, 1 atm) and about 24.0 L at RTP (25 °C, 1 bar).
Molar mass is numerically equal to the relative atomic or molecular mass when the latter is expressed in g mol⁻¹.
One mole of H₂SO₄ contains 7 moles of atoms in total — 2 mol H, 1 mol S and 4 mol O.
One mole of NaCl gives 1 mol Na⁺ and 1 mol Cl⁻, so 2 moles of ions altogether.
One mole of water is 18 g, or 18 mL of liquid, yet contains 6.022 × 10²³ molecules.

keyPoints: The mole is a counting unit, not a mass unit; it connects to mass only through the molar mass.
Always name the entity: 1 mol of O atoms is 16 g, but 1 mol of O₂ is 32 g and holds 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ atoms.
The 22.4 L molar volume applies only to ideal gases at STP; otherwise use PV = nRT.
Molar mass is in g mol⁻¹, while molecular or atomic mass is a relative number in u.
1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, which is one twelfth the mass of one ¹²C atom.
specialNotes: Since the 2019 SI revision N_A is a defined constant, 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹, rather than being derived from 12 g of ¹²C, so the older gram-atom style definition is outdated.

Molar masses rest on standard atomic weights, which are averages for natural isotopic composition and so carry an uncertainty; they vary slightly with source for elements such as boron, lithium and lead.
For an associating gas the particle count differs from the formula count, so n = V/22.4 L understates the true number of particles.
The mole expresses amount, not concentration: molarity, molality and mole fraction are different measures, and molarity alone is temperature-dependent because volume changes with temperature.
Mole-based stoichiometry cannot predict how fast a reaction proceeds, in which direction it goes, or what yield it gives — those come from kinetics, thermodynamics and equilibrium.
examShortTricks: Draw the four-way conversion web m ↔ n ↔ N ↔ V and use it as the framework of every numerical.
Mass of one molecule = M/N_A; multiply by the number of atoms per formula unit to get the total number of atoms.
Memorise key molar masses: H₂O 18, CO₂ 44, NaOH 40, CaCO₃ 100, H₂SO₄ 98 and NaCl 58.5 g mol⁻¹.
If the question says 'at STP', then 22.4 L per mole is valid; if any other T and P are given, switch to PV = nRT.
examNotes: This is the central topic of the stoichiometry unit, and a 5-mark numerical on any of the four relations is standard.

Limitations and the post-2019 exact value of N_A are frequently asked as short questions.
